model_justifications.haiku: Claim A identifies that input-label mapping impacts vary by experimental configuration, including language model size. model_justifications.haiku: Claim B identifies specific conditions (long-tailed distribution, increased classes) where label smoothing loses effectiveness, qualifying Claim A's general statement that label smoothing impairs distillation by specifying when this occurs.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A states that input-label mappings have varying impacts depending on configuration (e.g., model size). Claim B specifies that small models specifically fail to learn these mappings.

model_justifications.haiku: Both claims show that demonstrations improve few-shot learning performance without requiring ground truth labels. Both identify format/structure and input/label space specification as key factors, not semantic content.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A states that input-label mapping impact varies by configuration (including model size). Claim B builds on this by specifying how instruction tuning affects that mapping capacity.

model_justifications.haiku: Both claims affirm that demonstrations improve performance. Claim A analyzes what aspects drive gains (input/label space specification); Claim B extends this to sequence labeling (NER) tasks with quantified performance improvements on specific datasets.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A discusses label smoothing's benefit in knowledge distillation under label noise, while Claim B identifies specific data distributions where label smoothing loses effectiveness generally.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A finds benefit in noisy distillation; Claim B identifies long-tailed/many-class settings where effectiveness is lost. Different conditions explain the divergence.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A states label smoothing of teacher is beneficial when distilling from noisy data. Claim B identifies specific conditions (long-tailed distribution, increased classes) where label smoothing loses effectiveness, narrowing the scope of when it helps.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A states that input-label mappings have varying impacts depending on configuration; Claim B provides a specific instance where large models are significantly impacted by flipped labels.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A states impact varies by configuration; Claim B specifies that for large models with flipped labels, the impact is negative. B contextualizes A's general finding.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A identifies that input-label mapping impacts vary by experimental configuration. Claim B demonstrates this variation empirically, showing how large models' performance on input-label mappings depends on label correctness (flipped vs. correct labels).

model_justifications.qwen: Claim A attributes gains to input/label space specification and format. Claim B attributes performance to Task Recognition and Task Learning mechanisms. They address different explanatory factors.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims show demonstrations aren't strictly necessary for performance. Claim A shows format/label space matter; Claim B extends this by distinguishing task recognition (pre-trained priors) from task learning (new mappings), providing mechanistic detail.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A establishes the trade-off between robustness and accuracy, while Claim B introduces a specific technique (Interpolated Adversarial Training) to mitigate this accuracy loss.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim B shows a specific method reduces the accuracy drop claimed in A, qualifying the general trade-off by demonstrating it can be mitigated under specific training conditions.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims affirm that adversarial training reduces standard accuracy. Claim A states robust models show decreased standard accuracy; Claim B demonstrates this decrease (178.1% increase in error) but shows it can be mitigated with their method.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A shows LMs capture input-label mappings with prior-free labels; Claim B extends this by showing large models can use these mappings to override semantic priors.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim B specifies that large models override priors using input-label mappings, qualifying Claim A's general statement by identifying model scale as the determining condition.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims affirm language models capture input-label correspondence. Claim A shows this occurs even without label-space demonstrations. Claim B specifies this ability emerges primarily with model scale, qualifying when the capability manifests.

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims identify scenarios where traditional adversarial training decreases performance; Claim B extends this by identifying the small sample size regime as a specific cause.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim B states adversarial training may hurt robustness in small sample regimes, qualifying the general benefit by specifying a condition where it fails.
model_justifications.haiku: Both discuss adversarial training's effects on accuracy. Claim A shows decreased accuracy with traditional adversarial training. The difference in data availability conditions explains the apparent opposition.

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims find label smoothing beneficial for knowledge distillation. Paper A focuses on noisy data settings, while Paper B argues it helps distinguish semantically similar classes.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that label smoothing is beneficial for knowledge distillation. Claim A states it is 'beneficial' with noisy data; Claim B calls the mechanism a 'merit' rather than a drawback.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims affirm that label smoothing is beneficial in knowledge distillation contexts. Claim A shows label smoothing of the teacher is beneficial when distilling from noisy data. Claim B argues erasing information via label smoothing is a merit for knowledge distillation, not a drawback.

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims show that demonstrations with random components (tokens or words) still provide significant performance improvements in few-shot/in-context learning scenarios.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that demonstrations with random/meaningless labels still significantly improve model performance, supporting the finding that ground truth alignment is not required for in-context learning benefits.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims show that demonstrations with random/non-meaningful labels still improve model performance in few-shot learning, supporting the same finding that label content is not essential for demonstration effectiveness.

model_justifications.gemini: Both papers explore conditions where label smoothing's effectiveness varies; Paper A focuses on noisy settings, while Paper B identifies long-tailed distributions and class counts as factors.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A addresses label smoothing in noisy distillation settings. Claim B addresses long-tailed distributions and class counts. They discuss different conditions affecting effectiveness.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A shows label smoothing helps distillation in noisy settings (opposite to Müller et al.). Claim B identifies specific conditions (long-tailed distribution, many classes) where label smoothing loses effectiveness, extending the nuanced understanding of when label smoothing helps or hurts.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim B provides a theoretical explanation (flat vs sharp minima) for the generalization gap between SGD and Adam that Claim A seeks to close with a new algorithm.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that SGD generalizes better than Adam. Claim A states the proposed method matches SGD and beats Adam; Claim B explains why SGD outperforms Adam.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims assert that SGD generalizes better than adaptive methods (Adam/Amsgrad). Claim A shows Padam achieves generalization 'as good as SGD with momentum and much better than existing adaptive gradient methods.' Claim B explains why SGD generalizes better than Adam. Both support the same finding about SGD's superior generalization.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A finds label smoothing improves student generalization in standard settings, while Claim B extends the benefit of label smoothing to teacher models in noisy data distillation.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim B contrasts findings for noisy data with noise-free problems, qualifying Claim A's general assertion that label smoothing improves generalization by specifying conditions.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims support label smoothing's benefits, but Claim B qualifies Claim A by specifying that label smoothing benefits differ between noisy and noise-free settings, providing contextual conditions for when it is beneficial.

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims assert that in-context labels impact performance, with Paper A specifying this impact varies by configuration and Paper B confirming ICL incorporates label information.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A states impact varies by configuration; Claim B asserts ICL generally incorporates label info. The variation in A contextualizes the general finding in B, explaining discrepancies without direct contradiction.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims affirm that ground-truth labels/label information significantly impact in-context learning performance. Claim A shows correct input-label mappings have varying impacts; Claim B shows ICL incorporates in-context label information and learns novel tasks.

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims assert that demonstrations with random components (tokens or sentences/labels) still provide significant performance gains in few-shot/in-context learning compared to standard demonstrations.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that demonstrations with random or irrelevant content still significantly improve model performance in few-shot/in-context learning settings.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims show that random/non-standard demonstrations still improve model performance in few-shot learning tasks, demonstrating that ground truth content is not necessary for demonstration effectiveness.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim B builds on the state-of-the-art performance established by models like Autoformer (Claim A), demonstrating further error reductions using a different architecture (FEDformer) across multiple datasets.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A reports Autoformer's MSE reduction on the ETT dataset. Claim B reports FEDformer's error reduction across six benchmarks. Different models and datasets.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A reports Autoformer's 14% MSE reduction on ETT dataset. Claim B reports FEDformer's 14.8% and 22.6% error reduction across six datasets. Different models, datasets, and metrics prevent direct comparison of the same relationship.

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims assert that smaller batch sizes (less accurate estimates of the full-batch gradient) improve performance or stability compared to larger batch sizes.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that smaller batch sizes improve performance or stability. Claim A states better gradient estimates (large batches) harm performance; Claim B states small batches improve convergence robustness.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims support that smaller batch sizes improve performance. Claim A shows improving gradient estimates (larger batches) can harm performance; Claim B extends this by demonstrating small batches provide stable convergence across wider learning rate ranges on multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet).

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims assert that adversarial training increases standard error, with Paper A showing this theoretically in linear regression and Paper B providing empirical evidence on CIFAR-10.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that adversarial training increases standard error. Claim B provides empirical evidence on CIFAR-10 supporting the phenomenon described theoretically in Claim A.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims affirm that adversarial training increases standard error. Claim A shows this theoretically in linear regression; Claim B demonstrates it empirically on CIFAR-10, supporting the same finding.

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims agree that models struggle to fully overcome semantic priors when labels are flipped; Paper A specifies this effect for instruction-tuned models versus standard ones.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that models struggle to override pre-training priors with flipped labels, evidenced by persistent performance gaps or inability to follow flipped targets.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A states large models can override semantic priors with flipped labels. Claim B states a significant gap between default and flipped label predictions remains even at maximum context size, indicating models cannot overcome pre-training preferences.

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims assert that smaller batch sizes (which increase SGD noise) lead to better generalization/test accuracy, consistent with the identified noise scale relationship.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that increased SGD noise (via smaller batch size) improves generalization. Claim A links this to Bayesian evidence; Claim B confirms it experimentally.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims assert that smaller batch size (increased SGD noise) improves generalization. Claim A proposes batch size affects generalization gap; Claim B empirically confirms smaller batch size leads to better generalization.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A establishes the accuracy-robustness trade-off, while Claim B identifies a specific cause (inductive bias mismatch) and proposes a mitigation strategy.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim B explains the mechanism (inductive bias mismatch) causing the standard error increase asserted in Claim A, extending the finding to noiseless linear regression.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims affirm that adversarial training/robustness causes standard accuracy/error to increase. Paper B extends Paper A by providing mechanistic explanation (inductive bias mismatch) for the phenomenon Paper A demonstrated empirically.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A identifies the 'over adaptation' problem in Adam/Amsgrad, while Claim B provides a theoretical explanation for why SGD generalizes better than Adam via flat minima.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that SGD generalizes better than Adam/adaptive methods in deep neural networks, aligning on the same relationship and direction.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims address why adaptive methods (Adam/Amsgrad) generalize worse than SGD. Claim A identifies 'over adaptation' as the problem; Claim B extends this by explaining the mechanism: adaptive methods find sharp minima while SGD finds flatter minima that generalize better.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim B identifies a specific cause (ineffective L2 regularization) for the poor generalization of adaptive methods observed in Claim A, thereby contextualizing the finding.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim B attributes Adam's poor generalization to ineffective L2 regularization, qualifying Claim A's general observation by identifying a specific cause and implying fixability.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claim adaptive methods generalize worse than SGD. Claim B identifies a specific cause (ineffective L2 regularization in Adam) and proposes a fix, qualifying rather than contradicting Claim A's general observation.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A shows label smoothing improves distillation under label noise, while Claim B finds weighted soft labels improve distillation performance by tuning bias-variance tradeoffs.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A assesses label smoothing's effect on distillation under noise. Claim B assesses weighted soft labels' effect via bias-variance tradeoff. Different methods and mechanisms.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A addresses label smoothing's effect on distillation under label noise. Claim B addresses weighted soft labels' effect on bias-variance tradeoff in distillation. Different methods (label smoothing vs. weighted soft labels) and different outcomes (noise robustness vs. bias-variance tradeoff).

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A specifies that certain types of labels (alphabetical/numerical) outperform others, while Claim B generally asserts the superiority of label words over non-label words.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A compares types of prior-free labels (alphabetical vs random). Claim B compares label words to non-label words generally. They address different relationships.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims affirm that label words/abstract labels outperform alternatives (random tokens/non-label words) in in-context learning, supporting the importance of appropriate label selection.

model_justifications.qwen: Claim A reports FEDformer's performance; Claim B reports CATS's performance. They describe different models' results, not the same relationship or direct comparison.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A reports FEDformer's MSE improvements on specific datasets. Claim B reports CATS model's MSE performance compared to existing models. Different models, different datasets, different comparisons—not the same relationship being evaluated.

model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that adversarial robustness techniques can lead to an increase in standard error (or decrease in accuracy), confirming the trade-off between robustness and standard performance.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims assert that adversarial training/robustness leads to increased standard error/decreased standard accuracy. Claim A states robust models show decreased standard accuracy; Claim B shows standard error increases with adversarial augmentation.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A identifies an inherent trade-off between accuracy and robustness, while Claim B builds on this by providing theoretical bounds and a specific algorithmic defense (TRADES).

model_justifications.haiku: Both papers affirm a robustness-accuracy trade-off. Paper B extends Paper A by providing theoretical characterization via classification-calibrated loss bounds and proposing the TRADES algorithm to manage this trade-off.

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims assert that adaptive methods like Adam can suffer from poor generalization compared to SGD, motivating the development of new optimizers to address this.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that adaptive methods like Adam suffer from poor generalization compared to SGD, motivating the development of new optimizers.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims assert that adaptive methods (like Adam) have convergence advantages but generalization problems compared to SGD, motivating development of improved optimizers.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A relates the learning rate/batch size ratio to minima width and generalization, while Claim B relates batch size to the range of stable learning rates.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A links generalization to the LR/batch ratio, while Claim B links convergence stability specifically to small batch sizes. They address different aspects (generalization vs. stability) and conditions.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A states higher learning rate/batch size ratio leads to better generalization. Claim B shows small batch sizes provide stable convergence with larger learning rate ranges. Both discuss batch size effects on training dynamics but under different optimization criteria (generalization vs. convergence stability).

model_justifications.gemini: Claim B explicitly cites and confirms the finding in Claim A that label smoothing in teacher models impairs knowledge distillation to student models.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim B accurately summarizes Claim A's finding that label smoothing impairs distillation, resulting in worse student model performance.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims assert that label smoothing impairs knowledge distillation when teacher models are trained with label smoothing, resulting in worse student model performance.

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims identify and analyze the same phenomenon: that Adam generalizes worse than SGD in deep learning contexts.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that Adam generalizes worse than SGD and the respective works analyze or address this specific generalization gap.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims identify and analyze why Adam generalizes worse than SGD. Paper A develops a variant to eliminate the gap; Paper B provides theoretical understanding of the gap through SDE analysis. Same core finding.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim B notes Adam's poor generalization compared to SGD; Claim A builds on this by identifying ineffective L2 regularization as a major factor for this gap.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that Adam generalizes poorly compared to SGD. Claim A identifies a cause, while Claim B states the observation; they agree on the relative performance.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims assert that Adam generalizes poorly compared to SGD. Claim A identifies L2 regularization ineffectiveness as a major factor; Claim B documents the poor generalization phenomenon itself.

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims assert that adaptive methods (like ADAM) generalize worse than non-adaptive methods (like SGD), with Paper B providing a theoretical explanation for Paper A's observation.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that adaptive methods (like Adam) generalize worse than SGD. Claim B's 'degeneration' aligns with Claim A's 'generalize worse'.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims assert that adaptive methods (AdaGrad, Adam, RMSProp) generalize worse than SGD. Claim A presents empirical experiments demonstrating this; Claim B analyzes the theoretical explanation for this same generalization gap.

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims agree that adaptive methods (like Adam) typically exhibit worse generalization performance compared to SGD, with Paper B providing a theoretical explanation for this observation.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that adaptive methods (like Adam) generalize worse than SGD. Claim A states this as a typical observation; Claim B analyzes this specific performance degeneration.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims affirm that adaptive methods (ADAM) generalize worse than SGD. Claim A states adaptive methods 'generalize worse compared to SGD'; Claim B analyzes 'generalization performance degeneration of ADAM-alike adaptive algorithms over SGD.'

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims assert that label smoothing is beneficial for knowledge distillation, with Paper A focusing on noisy data and Paper B focusing on distinguishing semantically similar classes.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that label smoothing is beneficial for knowledge distillation. Claim A states it 'improves performance,' while Claim B calls the mechanism a 'merit' rather than a drawback.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims affirm that label smoothing is beneficial for knowledge distillation. Claim A states it 'improves performance of distillation under label noise'; Claim B argues erasing information is 'a merit...for knowledge distillation, rather than a drawback.'

model_justifications.gemini: Paper A identifies the learning rate to batch size ratio as scaling noise; Paper B builds on this, proposing that this noise drives parameters toward specific minima.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that SGD noise (scaled by learning rate/batch size ratio) influences the properties of the final minima found.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims identify that noise (scaled by learning rate to batch size ratio) in SGD drives convergence to minima with desirable properties—wider minima with better generalization (A) and high Bayesian evidence (B).

model_justifications.gemini: Both papers address Adam's poor generalization compared to SGD. Paper A identifies L2 regularization inequivalence, while Paper B identifies different reasons and proposes a different variant (ND-Adam).
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A attributes poor generalization to L2 regularization ineffectiveness. Claim B states reasons are identified and a new variant (ND-Adam) is developed, without specifying the same cause.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims address Adam's poor generalization versus SGD. Claim A identifies L2 regularization ineffectiveness as a major factor; Claim B identifies reasons more broadly and proposes a solution (ND-Adam), extending the investigation to different causes and remedies.

model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that ResNet-50 on ImageNet can be trained with large batches while maintaining high accuracy, supporting the same finding.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims report training ResNet-50 on ImageNet to high accuracy using large batch sizes. Claim A achieves 76.1% in under 30 minutes on TPU; Claim B matches small minibatch accuracy in one hour on 256 GPUs. Same finding applied to different hardware/settings.

model_justifications.gemini: Both claims assert that their respective new Transformer-based models (Informer and PatchTST) outperform existing state-of-the-art models in long-term time-series forecasting.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A evaluates Informer's performance; Claim B evaluates PatchTST's performance. They concern different models, not the same relationship.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims report improved long-term forecasting performance with Transformer-based models. model_justifications.gemini: Paper A finds label smoothing improves general supervised learning models; Paper B extends this finding to the specific context of denoising and distillation under label noise.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim B extends Claim A's finding on label smoothing's benefits to the specific setting of label noise and distillation.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims affirm label smoothing improves model performance. Claim A shows improvement across standard benchmarks without hyperparameter modification. Claim B extends this to noisy label settings and distillation, demonstrating broader applicability.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A suggests labels don't matter for ICL, while Claim B finds large models can learn specific input-label mappings, qualifying A's findings based on model scale.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim B specifies that large models override priors using input-label mappings, qualifying Claim A's finding that random labels work by attributing it to scale-dependent emergent abilities.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A shows random labels retain 75-87% of ICL improvements, suggesting label content is not critical. Claim B shows large models override semantic priors with input-label mappings, implying label content matters for performance.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A links large batches to sharp minima and poor generalization; Claim B identifies the learning rate to batch size ratio as the mechanism controlling this noise.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A links sharp minimizers to poor generalization in large-batch methods. Claim B identifies the learning rate/batch size ratio as controlling dynamics via noise scaling. They address different specific relationships.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims support that batch size affects minima sharpness and generalization. Claim A: large batches → sharp minima → poor generalization. Claim B: learning rate/batch size ratio controls noise, affecting minima width and generalization. Both identify batch size as key factor influencing minima properties and generalization.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A demonstrates successful large-batch training on ImageNet, while Claim B extends the utility of large-batch training to transfer learning performance and Mask R-CNN.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A reports ImageNet accuracy for Inception-ResNet-V2. Claim B discusses transfer learning performance and Mask R-CNN. They address different models and outcomes.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims demonstrate successful large-batch training on ImageNet. Claim A shows 77% accuracy with 65536-image batches; Claim B extends findings to transfer learning with Mask R-CNN, showing large minibatches don't degrade performance when ImageNet error is matched.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A specifies that certain label types (alphabetical/numerical) improve ICL performance, while Claim B broadly asserts that ICL incorporates label information and learns novel tasks.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A compares label types (alphabetical vs random) in prior-free settings. Claim B asserts ICL incorporates label information generally. They address different aspects of label usage.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims affirm that language models can capture and utilize input-label correspondence in in-context learning, despite prior skepticism about label importance.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A proposes AdamW to improve Adam's performance. Claim B finds that tuned Adam (or variants like AdamW) provides stable, improved results across a benchmark.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A assesses decoupled weight decay's effect on generalization; Claim B assesses tuning Adam variants. Different interventions and outcomes.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A shows decoupled weight decay improves Adam's generalization on image classification. Claim B extends this by demonstrating tuned Adam variants provide stable, improved results across many different benchmark problems, validating the improvement in a broader experimental context.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A compares label smoothing to dropout regarding gradient norms and convergence. Claim B compares Beta smoothing to label smoothing and self-distillation regarding performance/accuracy.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A discusses gradient norms and convergence speed; Claim B discusses predictive performance accuracy. They assess different outcomes.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A discusses gradient norms and convergence speed of label smoothing versus dropout. Claim B compares performance of Beta smoothing versus label smoothing on specific datasets. Different outcomes measured.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A discusses how increasing adversarial training intensity can hurt robust accuracy, while Claim B focuses on reducing standard error using a specific interpolation technique.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A analyzes standard adversarial training's effect on robust accuracy. Claim B evaluates a different method, Interpolated Adversarial Training, focusing on reducing standard error increase.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims address adversarial training's effect on standard error. Claim A observes the problem; Claim B extends by proposing Interpolated Adversarial Training as a solution that mitigates the standard error increase while maintaining robustness.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A reports an accuracy drop using traditional adversarial training, while Claim B argues this tradeoff is not inherent but a limitation of current methods.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that the robustness-accuracy tradeoff stems from current training methods rather than being inherent, with Claim A providing a specific example of this methodological limitation.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A shows traditional adversarial training decreases accuracy; Claim B argues the tradeoff results from current method limitations, not inherent constraints. AdvProp (Claim A's method) represents an improved training approach addressing Claim B's identified limitations.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A suggests augmenting robust training with generalization techniques to achieve accuracy; Claim B demonstrates this by using interpolation-based training to improve generalization while preserving robustness.
model_justifications.qwen: Both claims assert that augmenting robust training with generalization techniques improves accuracy without sacrificing robustness. Claim B extends this by validating a specific interpolation-based method.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims assert that augmenting robust training methods with generalization techniques achieves both robustness and accuracy. Claim A proposes local Lipschitzness + generalization techniques; Claim B demonstrates interpolation-based augmentation preserves robustness while improving generalization.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A compares Beta smoothing to label smoothing and self-distillation, while Claim B discusses the benefits of label smoothing for teachers when distilling from noisy data.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A compares Beta smoothing to self-distillation/label smoothing on clean data. Claim B discusses label smoothing's benefit in distillation under label noise. Different methods and conditions.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A compares Beta smoothing to label smoothing and self-distillation on clean datasets. Claim B examines label smoothing's effectiveness in distillation under label noise. Different conditions (noise-free vs. noisy data) and different relationships (smoothing technique comparison vs. teacher label smoothing benefit).

model_justifications.gemini: Claim B provides specific evidence of large-batch training difficulties (with ADAMW on BERT) that aligns with Paper A's general observation of a generalization gap in large-batch regimes.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A discusses generalization gaps and sharp minima in large-batch SGD. Claim B reports ADAMW's failure on large-batch BERT training. They address different optimizers and outcomes.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A discusses strategies to improve large-batch generalization despite sharp minima. Claim B reports ADAMW optimizer failure in large-batch BERT training. Different methods and outcomes are addressed.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A asserts that label smoothing improves model performance, while Claim B focuses on a stability metric for evaluating information erasure by label smoothing in knowledge distillation.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A asserts label smoothing improves model performance. Claim B proposes a metric aligned with accuracy for teacher selection in knowledge distillation. They address different relationships.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A asserts label smoothing improves models without hyperparameter modification. Claim B proposes a metric to evaluate erased information by label smoothing for knowledge distillation. Different outcomes and methods examined.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A compares label smoothing to confidence penalty in machine translation, while Claim B identifies specific conditions (long-tailed distributions, many classes) where label smoothing loses effectiveness.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A compares label smoothing to confidence penalty in machine translation. Claim B identifies conditions where label smoothing loses effectiveness. They address different relationships.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A compares label smoothing vs. confidence penalty performance on machine translation. Claim B identifies conditions where label smoothing loses effectiveness (long-tailed distribution, many classes). Different relationships: relative performance vs. effectiveness conditions.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A discusses the impact of random labels on ICL performance, while Claim B focuses on how instruction tuning affects a model's reliance on semantic priors.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A concerns retaining performance with random labels; Claim B concerns instruction tuning increasing reliance on semantic priors. Different factors and outcomes.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A reports retention of ICL improvements using random English words paired with inputs. Claim B discusses instruction tuning's effect on semantic priors versus input-label mappings. Different experimental setups and outcomes being measured.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A compares Beta smoothing to label smoothing and self-distillation, while Claim B discusses the effect of weighted soft labels on distillation performance.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A compares Beta smoothing to label smoothing/self-distillation. Claim B discusses weighted soft labels and teachers trained with label smoothing. Different methods.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A compares Beta smoothing to label smoothing and self-distillation. Claim B discusses weighted soft labels improving distillation performance. Different methods and outcomes are being evaluated.

model_justifications.gemini: Paper A finds label smoothing improves general model performance, while Paper B extends this finding to show its effectiveness in coping with label noise.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A assesses improvement on standard benchmarks; Claim B assesses effectiveness against label noise. Different outcomes/conditions.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims affirm label smoothing improves model performance. Claim A shows improvement across clean-data benchmarks; Claim B extends this to noisy-label settings, demonstrating label smoothing's effectiveness in a different condition.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A asserts Informer's superior performance in LSTF, while Claim B asserts a newer model (CATS) achieves superior performance and lower error than existing models (including Informer).
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A evaluates Informer's performance; Claim B evaluates CATS's performance. They assess different models, not the same relationship.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claim improved forecasting performance across datasets. Claim A reports Informer's success in LSTF with smooth error growth. Claim B reports CATS achieves superior performance with lower MSE and fewer parameters, suggesting architectural improvements beyond Informer's approach.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim B states Adam generalizes worse than SGD, while Claim A proposes a modification (AdamW) that allows Adam to compete with SGD, contextualizing the generalization gap.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim B states Adam generalizes worse than SGD. Claim A confirms this was the prior state ('previously typically outperformed') before their modification improved it.
model_justifications.haiku: Both claims address Adam's generalization gap versus SGD with momentum. Claim A reports that decoupled weight decay improves Adam to compete with SGD with momentum. Claim B identifies the generalization gap problem that Claim A's solution addresses.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A discusses the performance of the LARS optimizer on ResNet-50 and AlexNet, while Claim B discusses the failure of the ADAMW optimizer on BERT.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A discusses LARS performance on ResNet-50; Claim B discusses ADAMW failure on BERT. Different methods, models, and outcomes.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A discusses LARS performance on ResNet-50 with batch size 32K. Claim B discusses ADAMW optimizer failure on BERT with large batches. Different optimizers, different models, different tasks.

model_justifications.gemini: Paper A shows demonstrations (even random) improve few-shot learning, while Paper B extends this by showing large models can specifically override semantic priors using in-context mappings.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A focuses on random token demonstrations and superficial patterns. Claim B focuses on large models overriding semantic priors via input-label mappings. Different mechanisms.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A shows random token demonstrations improve few-shot learning despite lacking semantic content. Claim B shows large models override semantic priors with in-context mappings. These contradict: A suggests semantic content irrelevant; B suggests semantic priors are overridable by meaningful mappings.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A discusses PatchTST for time series forecasting, while Claim B discusses DeltaNet for language modeling. They address different models, tasks, and datasets.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A assesses PatchTST on time series forecasting; Claim B assesses DeltaNet on language modeling. Different methods, tasks, and domains.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A concerns time series forecasting performance on ETTh1 dataset using PatchTST. Claim B concerns language modeling perplexity and downstream task performance using DeltaNet. Different tasks, models, and evaluation metrics.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A discusses a trade-off between robustness and accuracy, while Claim B focuses on reducing the computational time required for adversarial training using a specific mechanism.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A addresses the accuracy-robustness trade-off. Claim B reports computational time savings. They assess different outcomes (accuracy vs. time).
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A addresses the theoretical tension between adversarial robustness and standard accuracy. Claim B reports computational efficiency improvements in adversarial training. These concern different outcomes (accuracy trade-off vs. training time).

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A establishes Autoformer's performance on specific datasets, while Claim B introduces iTransformer as a new state-of-the-art, building on the Transformer family's forecasting capabilities.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A reports Autoformer's specific performance on Exchange dataset. Claim B reports iTransformer's general state-of-the-art status. They concern different models and do not directly compare the same relationship.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A reports Autoformer's performance on Exchange dataset (17% MSE reduction). Claim B makes general claims about iTransformer's state-of-the-art performance without specifying datasets or metrics, making direct comparison impossible.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A discusses the theoretical insufficiency of flatness for explaining generalization, while Claim B introduces a specific algorithm (Ghost-BN) to improve generalization in large-batch training.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A discusses flatness and prediction function properties for generalization. Claim B introduces Ghost-BN to improve generalization. They address different methods/factors.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A discusses whether flatness of loss minima determines generalization ability. Claim B describes an algorithm (Ghost-BN) that improves generalization performance. These address different aspects of generalization—one about loss landscape properties, one about a training technique.

model_justifications.gemini: The claims describe performance improvements for two different models (PatchTST for time series vs. DeltaNet hybrids for language modeling) on entirely different tasks and datasets.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A concerns PatchTST for time series forecasting. Claim B concerns DeltaNet hybrids for language modeling. Different domains, models, and tasks.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A concerns PatchTST's performance on time series forecasting with self-supervised learning. Claim B concerns hybrid DeltaNet models' performance on language modeling tasks. Different domains, methods, and outcomes.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A discusses a calibration method to improve accuracy and reduce variance, while Claim B discusses the ability of GPT-3 to override semantic priors with flipped labels.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A assesses calibration's effect on accuracy/variance. Claim B assesses GPT-3's inability to override semantic priors with flipped labels. Different interventions and outcomes.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A addresses calibration improving accuracy and reducing variance in few-shot learning. Claim B addresses GPT-3's inability to override semantic priors with flipped labels. Different mechanisms and outcomes are examined.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A proposes a new label smoothing technique, while Claim B proposes a metric to evaluate information erasure by label smoothing for teacher selection.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A proposes a label smoothing technique promoting diversity. Claim B proposes a metric to measure erased information for teacher selection. They address different methods and outcomes.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A proposes an instance-specific label smoothing technique promoting diversity without separate teacher models. Claim B proposes a stability metric to evaluate erased information by label smoothing for identifying good teachers. Different methods and outcomes.

model_justifications.gemini: Claim A finds label smoothing improves models generally; Claim B extends this by showing weighted soft labels (a form of smoothing) improve performance via bias-variance tradeoffs.
model_justifications.qwen: Claim A addresses confidence penalty/label smoothing in supervised learning. Claim B addresses weighted soft labels in knowledge distillation. Different methods and settings.
model_justifications.haiku: Claim A addresses confidence penalty and label smoothing as regularizers in supervised learning. Claim B addresses weighted soft labels in knowledge distillation. Different methods and contexts.
